title: Knot stitch and bobble
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), fig. 354. Public domain. Bobble construction also drawn from Weldon's Practical Knitter series (1880s). Public domain.

glossaryTerms.definition: A small three-dimensional knob worked from a single stitch by increasing into it, working short rows across the extra stitches, then decreasing back to one stitch.

content.text: The secret of both the knot stitch and the
bobble

is that several loops are made from one stitch, then closed back to one loop. This traps extra yarn inside a small mound on the fabric surface. A knot stitch closes on the same row by passing earlier stitches over the last one. A bobble works a few short rows before closing, which makes a larger bump.

You need yarn, needles, and the ability to work knit and purl stitches. Bobbles are easier to learn in an aran or chunky weight where the action is visible; the same principle applies to finer weights once the motion is familiar.

content.text: Step by step
Knot stitch (closes on the same row):
On a right-side row, work to the position of the knot.
Into the next stitch, work (knit 1, purl 1, knit 1) without dropping the original stitch from the left needle. You have 3 new stitches from the one stitch.
Drop the original stitch from the left needle. You now have 3 stitches on the right needle where there was 1.
Pass the second stitch on the right needle over the third. Then pass the first stitch over the third. One stitch remains: the knot.
Bobble (MB: make bobble, using 5 stitches from 1):
On a right-side row, work to the bobble position.
Into the next stitch work (k1, p1, k1, p1, k1) without dropping the original stitch. 5 stitches from 1.
Turn the work so the wrong side faces you. Purl across the 5 bobble stitches only.
Turn. Knit across the 5 bobble stitches.
Turn. Purl 2 together, purl 1, purl 2 together. 3 stitches remain.
Turn. Slip 1, knit 2 together, pass the slipped stitch over. 1 stitch remains. The bobble is closed. Resume working across the main row.
Where you'll see it

Knot stitches appear in traditional lace and textured patterns as small surface details. Bobbles are a key part of Aran knitting. They sit among cable panels and stand for visual motifs such as blackberries and clover.
Common faults

Flat bobble. Working only 3 stitches instead of 5, or skipping the short rows entirely, produces a flat nub rather than a proud bobble. The short rows are what push the extra yarn forward into a dome.

Bobble sits sideways. If the short rows are worked for 3 rows rather than 2 (i.e., two knit rows and one purl row), the extra length tips the bobble to one side. Keep to the row count: 1 purl, 1 knit, 1 decrease purl, 1 decrease knit.
Loose tails beside the bobble. The yarn at each turning point within the bobble can leave a small loop at the base. Work the first stitch of each bobble row firmly to prevent this.
What to try next: work a bobble inside a cable panel. This is how Aran knitting combines texture and structure in the same row.
